1415.title: the summit sit
1415.hook: namah, namah, namah: a hymn that faces an angry god with a strung bow, and starts by bowing
1415.howItsDone: The Sri Rudram is chanted in Shiva temples and homes, often during abhisheka, when water, milk or other offerings are poured over the linga, and through the night of Maha Shivaratri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit read Nataraja all at once: the drum and the flame, held level.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `THE DRUM AND THE FLAME, LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Namah. Namah. Namah. Said once, it's a bow, a word of homage. Said over and over in a steady chant, it becomes a rhythm you can feel in the floor. The hymn built on it faces a god who is not, at first, gentle. Rudra stands with his bow strung and an arrow ready. And the hymn doesn't run, and doesn't argue. It bows: to the arrow, to the bow, to the anger itself. Today's summit sit climbs back to the Rudram, and the night the year spent awake with Shiva.
screen: `NAMAH, NAMAH, NAMAH.` → `A GOD WITH A STRUNG BOW.` → `THE HYMN BOWS.`

segments.voice: The Rudram comes from the Yajur Veda. In paraphrase, it opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, and to his arrow, and to his arms. Then it asks: make that arrow gentle; let your kind form be turned toward us. That's the first move. Fear isn't hidden or argued away. It's bowed to, and asked to soften. Then the hymn widens. It bows to Rudra in the short and the tall, the eldest and the youngest. In the trees with green hair. In the rain and in the drought, in the well and in the foam on the water. In thieves, even, and in the carpenters and the potters. Line after line, namah, until almost nothing in the world is left out of the bowing. Rudra isn't only on the mountain. He's in the crowd, the weather and the workshop. Then its companion, often chanted right after, turns the direction. Line after line, it asks: and to me, strength, food, breath, peace, long life. Bowing to everything, then asking honestly for what a person needs. The year carried that hymn into the dark, too. On Maha Shivaratri, it's chanted while water pours over the linga, through a night kept awake, often without food, until the gray light comes. From up here, the shape of the Shiva stretch is clearer. A god who frightens, faced by a hymn that bows. A bowing so wide it takes in the potter and the thief. And a long night where the only thing to do is stay awake and keep bowing.
screen: `BOW TO THE ANGER. ASK THE ARROW TO SOFTEN.` · `NAMAH TO THE TREES, THE RAIN, THE POTTER.` · `AND TO ME: AN HONEST ASK.` · `A NIGHT KEPT AWAKE.` · then, large: `NOTHING LEFT OUT OF THE BOWING.`

segments.voice: Let the bow move outward, one thing per breath: your own body, the room, the people nearby, the weather outside, someone who makes you angry. If something feels too hard to bow to, bow to the hard feeling instead; if you pray, say namah softly with each one.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the Rudram and Shivaratri, a hymn that bows to an angry god and then to everything. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. The hymn bows first, then asks the arrow to soften. Until tomorrow.

1416.title: the summit sit
1416.hook: one ordinary Tuesday, looked at through each of the schools of thought the year walked through
1416.howItsDone: The darshanas are studied in traditional schools and universities through their root texts and commentaries, and each school's teachers answer the others' arguments in their own commentaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to the Rudram, a hymn that bows to an angry god, then to everything.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `BOW, AND ASK IT TO SOFTEN.`

segments.voice: A Tuesday morning. The coffee is late, the bus is later, and a message arrives that could mean two different things. Nothing special. But this path spent weeks handing that kind of morning to one school of thought after another, and each school saw something different in it. One asked how you know what the message means. One asked what the morning is made of. One asked who is watching it all happen. Today's summit sit climbs back to the schools of thought, the darshanas, and lays them side by side, with none on top.
screen: `A LATE BUS AND AN UNCLEAR MESSAGE.` → `ONE MORNING, MANY SCHOOLS.` → `NONE ON TOP.`

segments.voice: The word darshana means seeing, or a view; the same word is used for seeing the deity in a temple. So a school of thought, in this sense, is a way of looking. Run the Tuesday through them. Nyaya, the school of logic, asks first: how do you know? Is that message an insult, or a rushed typo? Nyaya says to hold the reason up to the light, like a bank teller with a note, before you act on it. Vaisheshika asks what there is: the cup, its warmth, its motion as you lift it, the self that notices, a careful list of kinds of things, all the way down. Samkhya points at a witness. The morning plays like a film, and someone is watching it, untouched by the plot. Yoga takes that map and laces up its boots: the angry reply, half typed, is a wave in the mind, and practice lets it settle. Mimamsa asks what you are being asked to do, and how a small act done right carries meaning past the moment. And Vedanta asks what, under all of it, is real, and its great teachers answer in more than one way. Here's what the year insisted on. These schools disagree, sometimes sharply, and their teachers argued with each other in long, careful books. The path didn't crown a winner, and it won't now. Each is a lens that brings something into focus. You can pick one up for an hour, set it down, and see the same Tuesday more clearly for it.
screen: `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · `NYAYA: HOW DO YOU KNOW?` · `SAMKHYA: WHO IS WATCHING?` · `VEDANTA: WHAT IS REAL?` · then, large: `LENSES, NOT RANKS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing from today that bothered you, and look at it first through Nyaya: how do I actually know what happened? Then set that lens down and pick up Samkhya, noticing the one who watches the bother and is not the bother itself. No need to decide which view is right; just notice how the moment changes as the lens changes.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the darshanas, the schools of thought, each a way of seeing, none ranked above the others. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Lenses, not ranks. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1417.title: the summit sit
1417.hook: a king finally sits down to eat after a long fast, and the guests keep coming
1417.howItsDone: Hindus practice seva in many forms: cooking and serving food at temples, caring for the sick and elderly, or working in the community, offered as service to God rather than for reward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit laid the schools of thought side by side: each a way of seeing, none on top.

The plate is finally in front of him. King Rantideva and his family have gone without food for a long time, and now there's a little rice, a little ghee, some water. He lifts his hand to eat. A knock. A hungry guest. The king shares. Another knock, another guest. He shares again. Then a man arrives with his dogs, all of them hungry. Today's summit sit climbs back to the lineage track, and the stretch on karma and seva: work, and work given away.
screen: `THE PLATE, FINALLY.` → `A KNOCK. ANOTHER KNOCK.` → `WORK, GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's how the Bhagavata finishes the story, in paraphrase. The king gives the man with the dogs everything that's left, and bows to him and to the dogs. Only the water remains. Then one more person comes, an outcaste by the rules of the day, thirsty, asking for a drink. The king gives him the water and says something. He doesn't want great powers from God, he says, and doesn't even ask to be freed from rebirth. He asks to enter the sorrow of all beings and carry it, so they can be free of it. Then the story turns: the guests were gods come to test him. They show themselves, and he asks them for nothing. Hold that next to the rest of the track. In the Uddhava Gita, a wandering beggar has his bowl snatched away, and he blames no one, not people, not the gods, not even karma, only the grip of his own mind. In the Gita, Krishna says the true renouncer isn't the one who quits his work and lets the fire go out, but the one who does the needed work without leaning on what it brings back. And seva: service, offered as worship. From up here, the track says something simple and hard. Karma isn't just a ledger of what comes back to you. It's work done without clutching the result, and seva is that work when the result goes to someone else. Rantideva's meal fed a guest, a stranger, a man with dogs and a thirsty outcaste, and when the gods stood before him, he had nothing left to ask for.
screen: `THE LAST OF THE WATER, GIVEN.` · `THE BOWL SNATCHED, NO ONE BLAMED.` · `DO THE WORK, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.` · `SEVA: WORK WHOSE FRUIT GOES TO ANOTHER.` · then, large: `NOTHING LEFT TO ASK FOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary piece of work you'll do today, a shift, a meal, a report, a ride for someone. On an out-breath, let your shoulders drop as if setting down what it will bring you, the thanks, the credit, the result; keep the work, let the fruit go, and if you pray, offer the work to God before you begin.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today: karma and seva, and a king who gave away his last cup of water. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. The work stays in your hands; the fruit can go to someone else. Rest well.

1418.title: the summit sit
1418.hook: rain, a dark narrow shelter, three strangers pressed together, and then a fourth who wasn't there before
1418.howItsDone: The hymns of the Alvars are sung in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes in Tamil Nadu, and the Narada Bhakti Sutras are studied and recited by devotees of many bhakti traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to karma and seva, and a king who gave away his last cup of water.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `THE LAST CUP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Rain is coming down hard at night. A wandering devotee ducks into a tiny shelter by a house. A second traveler knocks, and the first makes room. A third arrives, soaked, and the two make room again, and now they stand shoulder to shoulder. And then, tradition says, they feel a fourth pressing in among them, someone none of them can see. That's the story told of the first Alvars, the Tamil singers of Vishnu. Today's summit sit climbs back to the bhakti stretch, and the lamps those three lit.
screen: `RAIN, AND A TINY SHELTER.` → `ROOM MADE, AND MADE AGAIN.` → `A FOURTH, PRESSING IN.`

segments.voice: In the story, each sings a verse to light the dark. The first, Poygai, makes a lamp of the world: the earth for its bowl, the ocean for its oil, the sun for its flame. The second, Bhutam, makes a lamp of the heart: love for the bowl, longing for the oil, a melting mind for the wick. And the third, Pey, by that light, says simply: I have seen. The Lord is there, with the goddess, in the crowded dark. Now hold that next to the Narada Bhakti Sutras, the short book the year read whole. Its boldest claim is that bhakti, love for God, isn't the road to something else. It is where the road goes. Love is its own fruit. And when the sutras try to say what that love is like, they give up gracefully: it can't be told, like a taste in the mouth of someone who can't speak. You can have it. You can't hand it over in words. From up here, the shelter and the sutras say one thing in two keys. The singers don't argue their way to God. They light lamps and look, and the lamps are made of what they already have: the whole world, for one, their own love, for another. Then think of the women of the bhakti stretch, and the singers of the regions: a tailor, a cobbler, a weaver, singing to God in a home language. The shelter was too small. They made room anyway. And that, the story says, is when God pressed in.
screen: `A LAMP MADE OF THE WORLD.` · `A LAMP MADE OF LOVE.` · `LOVE IS ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `A TASTE THAT CAN'T BE TOLD.` · then, large: `THEY MADE ROOM ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Notice how full the mind is, the way the shelter was full, and without pushing anything out, make a little room on each out-breath, the way the first traveler shifted over for the second. If you pray, let that room be for God, as the Alvars felt someone press in; if you don't, let it be room for whoever comes next today.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: bhakti, the Alvars' lamps in a crowded shelter, and a love the sutras call its own fruit. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. A small shelter, and still room for one more. Until tomorrow.

1419.title: the summit sit
1419.hook: a glint in the wet sand at low tide, and a shell that was a shell the whole time
1419.howItsDone: Students of Advaita Vedanta study the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher, and pair the study with reflection and meditation on what the self is.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit stood with the Alvars in a crowded shelter, and a love that is its own fruit.

Low tide, late afternoon. Something in the wet sand catches the sun and flashes, bright as a dropped coin. A walker bends down for it. It's a shell, the inside of it shining. Nothing about the shell changed when it was picked up. It was a shell the whole time. What changed was the seeing. Shankara chose very nearly this picture to open his commentary on the Brahma Sutras. Today's summit sit climbs back to the last stretch of the lineage track: jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A GLINT IN THE SAND.` → `ONLY A SHELL.` → `THE SEEING CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Before he comments on a single line of the Brahma Sutras, Shankara writes a preface about that shell: mother-of-pearl taken for silver, one thing mistaken for another. His teaching is that a mistake like this sits at the root of bondage: taking the body and the mind, which come and go, for the self. Gaudapada, in his verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, gives the same kind of picture. On a dim path, a rope is taken for a snake. The fear is real. The snake isn't. What ends the fear isn't fighting the snake or running from it. It's seeing. When the rope is seen as rope, the snake doesn't leave. It was never there. The Brahma Sutras themselves open with a word that sounds almost casual: now. Now, then, the wish to know Brahman. In his comment on the fourth sutra, Shankara says freedom isn't produced, the way a pot is made from clay. It's what is already so, uncovered, the way the shell was always a shell. Gaudapada's last picture is a firebrand whirled in the dark, drawing circles that aren't there. Hold the stick still, and the circles stop. From up here, jnana looks less like piling up information and more like a light coming on. Not everyone on the path reads it this way. Ramanuja, whom the year also read, holds the world and the selves in it as real, the body of God, not a mistake to be seen through. But on the jnana track, the work is this: look closely enough, and what frightened you turns out to be rope.
screen: `THE SHELL TAKEN FOR SILVER.` · `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `NOW, THEN, THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THE FIREBRAND HELD STILL.` · then, large: `IT WAS ALWAYS ROPE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one worry that has been coiled on your path lately, and instead of fighting it, look at it more closely, the way a flashlight would: what exactly is there, and what have you added in the dim light? Stay with plain seeing for a while, then let the worry rest and rest as the one who sees; if you pray, ask for clear sight.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: jnana, the path of knowing, and the rope that was only ever rope. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Nothing about the shell changed; the seeing did. See you tomorrow.

1420.title: the summit sit
1420.hook: the sky going pale over a parking lot, and a Vedic singer who saw the same light and gave it a name
1420.howItsDone: Vedic hymns are recited from memory in traditional schools of chanting, and Hindus who keep a morning practice may greet the day with prayers such as the Gayatri, often facing the rising sun.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to jnana, and a rope that was only ever rope.

Early, before the alarm. Out the window, the sky over the parking lot goes from black to gray to something like the inside of a peach. A delivery truck idles. A bird starts, then another. Nobody will write a hymn about this morning. But weeks of this year went into hymns that did exactly that, sung to the fire, to the storm, to the dark before creation, and to this light. Today's summit sit climbs back to the Vedas themselves, and to Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `BLACK, GRAY, PEACH.` → `A BIRD, THEN ANOTHER.` → `USHAS, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, the dawn is a goddess, and the singers talk to her like someone they know. In one hymn, in paraphrase, she wakes every living thing and sends each off to its own work: one to look for food, one to its task, one to its prayer. She travels the same path every morning, never wearing out. Then the singer turns a corner. The people who watched the dawns before us are gone, the hymn says. We are the ones seeing her now, and others will come after us who will see her too. A hymn about light, and about being alive for a while. From up here, look how much of the Vedas stretch was like that. The very first hymn of the Rig Veda calls on Agni, the fire. Vasishtha asks Varuna why their friendship went cold. A hymn quotes, out loud, the people who doubt Indra exists. The hymn of creation ends with or perhaps not. The Sama Veda sets verses to song. The Atharva Veda sits at a sickbed with a glass of water. And the Gayatri turns out to be a verse to Savitr, the sun as the one who sets things moving. The year found that the Vedas aren't only ancient rules. They are people talking to the world as if it could hear: the fire, the water, the dark and the morning. Ushas is one door into all of it. She arrives every day. Nobody has to believe anything to see her come.
screen: `THE DAWN WAKES EVERY LIVING THING.` · `THOSE BEFORE US, US, THOSE AFTER.` · `FIRE, VARUNA, DOUBT, A SICKBED.` · `TALKING TO THE WORLD AS IF IT HEARS.` · then, large: `SHE ARRIVES EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Look at the light in a window, whatever the hour, or remember the last sunrise you saw. Bring to mind those who watched dawns before you, a grandparent, someone gone, and those who will see dawns after you, and sit in the middle of that line; if you pray, greet the dawn as the singers did. If missing someone weighs heavy today, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the Vedas themselves, and Ushas, the dawn who wakes every living thing. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Every dawn has had its watchers; this one has you. Same time tomorrow.

1421.title: the summit sit
1421.hook: a checkup that ends with 'you're fine', and an old definition of health that doesn't stop at the body
1421.howItsDone: Some Hindus draw on Ayurvedic ideas in daily life, through a morning routine, seasonal eating, or attention to sleep, alongside modern medicine; people who practice yoga often work with slow, unforced breathing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to the Vedas, and Ushas, the dawn who wakes every living thing.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `THE DAWN, BEFORE THE SCREEN.`

segments.voice: The paper gown, the cold stethoscope, the blood pressure cuff that squeezes a little too long. At the end, the doctor glances at the chart and says: you're fine. That's good news. But you're fine, there, mostly means nothing is wrong. Something missing, something broken: none found. Months back, this path spent a stretch with a classical tradition that asked a different question. Not what's wrong with you, but what does it look like when you're well? Today's summit sit climbs back to Ayurveda, read as a lens, and to the breath.
screen: `A COLD STETHOSCOPE.` → `YOU'RE FINE.` → `WHAT DOES WELL LOOK LIKE?`

segments.voice: First, what the year was careful to say. Ayurveda here was a way of noticing, not a diagnosis, and nothing in it replaces a doctor. With that said, look back. The doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, were read like weather: dry and moving, hot and sharp, heavy and steady, words for noticing how a day or a body feels. The Charaka Samhita's daily round started before dawn, cleaned the teeth and the tongue, oiled the body like a new cricket bat, and said to exercise only to half your strength. It also said to greet people first. Charaka named supports of life, and food and sleep were two of them. Then the breath, with every claim checked: Patanjali asks for breath that is long and subtle, not forced. Now the summit view. One classical definition of the healthy person, in the Sushruta Samhita, lists the body in balance: its doshas, its digestive fire, its tissues, its wastes. Then, in paraphrase, it doesn't stop there. It ends with a self, senses and mind that are clear and content. Health, in that definition, reaches all the way to whether the mind is at ease. That's why it fit on a path like this one. And it fits the end of this week: the Rudram, the schools of thought, karma and seva, bhakti, jnana, the Vedas, and now this. Different languages for the same climb: a person trying to live well, inside and out.
screen: `A WAY OF NOTICING, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.` · `THE DAILY ROUND: HALF YOUR STRENGTH.` · `BREATH, LONG AND SUBTLE.` · `HEALTH ENDS WITH A MIND AT EASE.` · then, large: `WELL, NOT JUST NOT SICK.`

segments.voice: Notice the breath as it is, without changing anything, then let the out-breath grow a little longer and quieter, long and subtle, not big and loud, letting it go back to normal if it strains. At the end, ask the old question gently: are the senses at ease, is the mind content, even a little? Don't fix anything; just notice.

The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Ayurveda as a lens, the breath made long and subtle, and a definition of health that ends with a mind at ease. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Well, not just not sick. A week on the summit, done.
